This is what was confusing to us as well because it seemed to us that the witness was moving from one place to the other, but once we determined the exact coordinates it turned out that these were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, you returned to your house from Pask Markaj's house soon after the war was over. Can you remember the precise date?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th, I think it was, of June, in the morning, because the army, the foreign army, entered Gjakova at midnight, and in the morning we returned to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your house was not damaged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not burnt, but all the furniture, everything that was there, everything was taken away. The equipment, the machinery we had, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the furniture, is it correct that at the beginning of the war you transferred some of your furniture to Dragutin Prentic's house for safekeeping?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before, much earlier, because I was afraid that they might come to my home in the night and set it ablaze. So it is true that I transferred a few precious pieces of furniture to his home and left it there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And he returned those items. They were preserved indeed.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the war ended Dragutin Prentic's house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that several houses were set on fire? That family possessed three houses, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. They had three small houses, and the three of them were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who set his house on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when his house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about the exact date. It may be some -- over 20 days after liberation. I have not correct information about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you don't know who set his house on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is I don't. Had -- had I known, I wouldn't have let anyone do that, because I might have let my brother live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, didn't you tell us today that everything that was inside Dragutin Prentic's house you see from your own front yard, and you described in some detail the events from 1998? How is it possible, Mr. Pnishi, that you didn't see the moment when the house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done at night. How could I see it during night?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, on the 6th of March, 1998, at 10.30 p.m. it was also dark when the house of Dragutin Prentic was shot at, and that's when you saw that. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time I couldn't have a wink of sleep at night for six months on end. I kept watch of what was happening. I was afraid less someone might come and kill us and burn us alive. But after the war, of course I could sleep. I slept better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pnishi, this is March, 1998. It wasn't wartime. I'm talking about the 6th of March, 1998. But let us move on to another question. You said that Dragutin Prentic's house was set on fire during the night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And I put it to you that one house was set on fire on one day and the remaining two houses the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the daylight. It was during night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, are you trying to tell me that you were in your house sleeping tight, whereas not even 50 metres away there was someone setting your neighbour's house on fire? Is that what you're trying to tell me?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sleeping, and when the -- I saw the flames. I couldn't -- of course, how do you think I could sleep tight seeing the flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Pnishi, that items were taken out of Dragutin Prentic's house before the house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone who didn't have a house moved in and lived there. Then I haven't seen anyone taking anything out of that house, and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Although this was in your immediate proximity, although that was your immediate neighbour, and although you stated here that you could see from your house everything that was happening in their house and in their front yard -- let's stop there. Is that correct first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying not to somebody. It's a matter of precision. If he's going to quote what the witness said then he should quote it correctly. The witness did not say that he could see everything that was happening inside the house. The witness could say that he saw them take somebody into the house and heard shots after. He did not say he could see everything that was happening inside the house. And there is something else. In any case, the question about whether or not he could see what happened to -- to Prentic's house has been asked four or five times in different formats. The witness has denied it. He didn't see what happened. I don't know how many times counsel should be permitted to ask the same question in different forms, so many times. There are time issues here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the only matter there that I would be concerned about, Mr. Visnjic, in relation to this particular question is whether you've properly asserted that the witness said he could see everything that was happening in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's told us what he could see, and we know that. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 18, he said, "[In English] He could see into my courtyard and I could see into his courtyard." [Interpretation] When he was explaining what it was that he could see in Dragutin Prentic's house and vice versa. I may have been imprecise as to the events taking place inside the house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your question goes as far as to say -- you put it on the basis that he could see into the house and the courtyard, and that's what -- that's the point that's being made by Mr. Stamp. He could see everything in the house and the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept that I may not have been very precise, but within the context of the fact that the house is set on fire from the outside, not from the inside, I have a question, a very direct question for Mr. Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, that is, it is my submission, impermissible comment, the context that it was set on fire from the outside and not from the inside. I don't know Defence will bring later on but the witness has accepted that it was set on fire from the inside -- from the outside or from the inside. There has been no evidence as to where the fire originated from. That is comment which is not based on evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Visnjic, perhaps you could clarify that with the witness first of all and then we could move on. Just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is a question of common sense. It's very hard for me to believe that somebody sets a house on fire from the inside and stays within.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, did you see anybody in the courtyard of the Prentic house when the house was torched?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not even at home when that house was set ablaze. I haven't seen anyone. I wasn't there when it was burned. I came after three, four hours, when the first was set ablaze, whereas when the second house was set on fire I was sleeping, and then when I saw the flames, I woke up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did the person by the name of Prenan [phoen] Pnishi participate in the torching of the Prentic house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have any such person. It's non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Prend Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prend Pnishi. It is not there. It was my brother who died 25 years ago. There is nobody by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about Kole Pnishi? Did he participate in the torching of the Prentic house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never. For the life of me, he would never have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Engjell Markaj, did he participate in the torching of the Prentic house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, I can guarantee you, sir, that no one from that area, Meja Orize, would have done that. I say this in full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you did not see who actually did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. Witness Pnishi, thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pnishi. I am Branko Lukic, and together with Dragan Ivetic and Ozren Ogrizovic I represent General Lukic in this courtroom. I'll try and clarify certain things with you, and I'll also try to put concise questions to you, and I call for your concise answers. My time is limited, and I would kindly ask you to understand that I will be forced to interrupt some of your answers. And if the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that you have to finish your answer, the Trial Chamber will ask you to do that. You were a policeman. In 1983, you retired from the police force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a retired policeman, for how long did you receive your retirement pay?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received pension until 1999, the 1st of January or February, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a retired police officer you were familiar with the structure of the SUP and of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, are you aware of the fact that at the critical time the chief of the SUP in Djakovica was Milovan Kovacevic? If you know, say so. If you don't, just say no.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that the chief of the crime prevention department within the police was Milan Stanojevic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the chief of the uniformed police was Radomir Colic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colic, I knew him somehow. Colic. I know him a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you spoke about Milutin Prascevic on page 2, paragraph 2 of your statement in B/C/S, and the same page and paragraph applied to the English and Albanian versions as well, you put Mr. Prascevic in the position of the chief of the crime prevention police. We have just established that Milan Stanojevic held that position. Before me I have death certificate for Prascevic, which says that he was just a police officer, nothing more. Does that jog your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the others I don't know, but for him I know that he was the head of the unit, and he did anything that he wanted to do, and this is known to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was the chief of a unit, what unit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- I'm talking about beating people, killing people, doing whatever he wanted and nobody could tell him stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What unit are you referring to? What are you talking about when you say that he was the head of a unit, that Prascevic was the head of a unit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know what he was, but he did whatever he wanted to do. He was like the boss of bosses, and he could do anything and no one could tell him to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that what you stated in your statement is not correct? The statement was given on the 4th of April, 2000. That's the statement I'm referring to, which is Exhibit 2236, the Prosecutor's Exhibit 2236. And when I say that, I mean that Milutin Prascevic was the chief of the crime prevention department of the Djakovica MUP. The question may have been too long, Mr. Pnishi. Let me rephrase. Is it true that you actually don't know what was Prascevic's position within the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his position. He was civilian, in civilian clothing, and that was all the time. And he did anything that he wanted to do in the region of Gjakova, and everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you're talking about the killing of Milutin Prascevic on the transcript page 1441, lines 17 to 21, you say the following: "On the 22nd of April, around 5.00 in the afternoon, in Meja, the militant criminal Prascevic, with four men very much like him, was killed." In your view, is it the right thing for these people to have been killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about this when all the police and the military came to the area and they gathered there and we heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again I must interrupt you. You're not answering the question that you've been asked. Please listen to the question that's being asked. And you're being asked whether in your opinion you thought it was right that Prascevic and his colleagues were killed. In other words, was that a good thing in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, it's not good to kill anyone, but they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that among these men, among the five men, Naser Arifaj was also killed? He was an Albanian, a member of the local security guards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard about him, but I don't know who the man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were aware of the existence of the institution of local security in your area, in your village, of the local guards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our village. In other villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that these units were composed of local Albanians, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also know that they had special uniforms by which they recognised each other?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also know that these units were armed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that members of these units were selected or elected by the local population.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. They were selected by the Serbian police, not the people, not by the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that these units were not established by the police but, rather, by the municipal assemblies?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly selected them together with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, I would like to move on to another armed formation, and I would like to ask you something about the existence of the KLA in your area. In the area of your village and in the general area, were there KLA units? Were any of the KLA units operational in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area there haven't been any KLA units. In 1998, in other villages, yes, there were, but in 1999 there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the area of Lugu and Carragojs, all the way up to the Keqe river, actually, the KLA was operational and existed there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in 1998 there were units, but when the offensive took place in 1999 there weren't any units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for your testimony today that Prascevic and the other four policemen were killed by some of the locals of Meja, is that what you're saying or are you saying that this was done by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, can you repeat the question once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who killed Prascevic, in your view, as well as the other four police officers? Were they killed by the KLA or the locals of Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the KLA could not get to that area because on both sides there was the deployment of the Serbian army, and there were checkpoints every 100 metres and there were units deployed. I -- and I can tell you 100 per cent that none of the villagers or the KLA killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your testimony, that they -- they were fighting amongst each other? Can you tell us what you think? Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who killed him, they know it, because there are many cases like this that have taken place. And I don't know who killed them, but those who did it, they know it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You hail from Ramoc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm from Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Ramoc also part of the area that we have just mentioned, the area of Lug and Carragojs, all the way to the Carragojs river valley?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They're included in Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before me I have a list, and I'm going to ask you whether you know any of the people on that list. Nik Pnishi from Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nik Pnishi from Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Born on the 18th of May, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Arec [as interpreted], Nec [Realtime transcript read in error "Not from Nec"]. I don't know when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pal Pnishi from Ramoc, do you know him? He was born on the 17th of October, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from Nec too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know Kent Pnishi, born on the 9th of October, 1980, also from Nec village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's part of the same family. He's a member of the same family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mark Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if there might be something with the transcript. Perhaps the question could be asked again. Having regard to the last two answers, I'm wondering if the transcript correctly records the answer to the question at line 14 of page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Line 19 I beg your pardon he says no and looking at the other records I'm wondering if the record correctly reflects what the witness said. Perhaps it could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you could do it in re-examination if you wish. I don't see any need to interrupt the cross-examination. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pnishi, we have left it off with the person named Mark Pnishi, born on the 3rd of April, 1949, from Nec village, but born in Ramoc. Sir, do we have an answer to my question? Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What -- what answer do you want me to give?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the person?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, these persons, together with some other persons, make up a group of 42 people altogether whose names are on the criminal report in connection with terrorist activity which points to the fact that they belong to the KLA. Are you familiar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. What is this document you're referring to? "The criminal report in connection with terrorist activity." That sounds like a very voluminous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not that voluminous, Your Honour. It's composed on 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it dealing with a particular event?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on it does have some sort of explanation, not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has it been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you know, we are receiving documents on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may take a bit of convincing on that one in view of what's been happening here. Are you telling me that -- well, you tell me when you got this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very unsatisfactory, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the last two days, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it should have been disclosed should is not? When we resume after the break unless there's a satisfactory explanation you'll not be allowed to ask that question. We'll break now and we will resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, what is the position with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that Your Honours won't be satisfied because we have this document from April, I guess. I received it last night with two other documents, the new ones, but this one we have for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have not received the documents as yet, not even now, so we can't -- the position is that we would need to see the document and to review the document before we can say if we could proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We'll move on to something else, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pnishi, again I shall go back to Milutin Prascevic, very briefly. You knew this person from before; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know his parents?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was a well-known person in that region; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a well-known person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean, did many people know him, both Albanians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in the circle he lived, because he lived far from Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did he live, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Decan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are talking about Milutin Prascevic, or are you talking about his father?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I beg you pardon. There has been a misunderstanding and the fault is all mine. Did many Albanians and Serbs in the area know Milutin Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he lived in Djakovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 40, line 9 of today's transcript, you say, "Wherever you seek shelter from the bullets that are falling you feel safer." I assume that the same goes for bombs; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, yes. So?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 41, line 1, you say that at Cabrat there was a tank at every 50 metres and that that hill was constantly being bombed. Don't you think that in that case many tanks would have been destroyed very quickly had there been that kind of deployment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to tanks, the tanks were lined from Gjakova to Junik, Cabrat and upwards, but the tanks shelled the villages. The houses, they set fire to them, and then they -- some of them withdrew. I don't know in what direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There were two parts to that question. The other one was the suggestion that NATO were constantly bombing that site. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO bombed it when there were barracks, army barracks. In the case of Cabrat, there wasn't any army barracks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you saying they did or they did not bomb Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't bomb Cabrat. The NATO bombed only those places where army barracks were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the passage at page -- the beginning of page 41 does not bear the influence that the witness was saying bombing was there constant limit it was one of these double questions where it's actually very difficult to tell for sure what the answer relates to, but all you can take from that answer is that the witness said that Cabrat hill was where you could find a tank stationed every 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that the witness clarified that his position is that Cabrat was not bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that the soldiers asked your son to show his ID; right? The Russian soldiers, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that they returned the ID because they didn't know how to read the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your son have an Albanian ID or a Serbian ID?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: An Albanian ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he did not have an ID of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time the IDs were written in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that a Serbian ID was written out only in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian inhabitants received it in Albanian language, whereas the Serbs in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd just like to ask you something about what you referred to on page 3, last paragraph in the B/C/S version. Just a moment, please. We'll find the other versions very quickly too. Last paragraph of page 3 in the English version, and then it continues on the page after that. And the third paragraph on page 4 of the Albanian language version. Here you say that four soldiers torched your brother's house. On transcript page 106 from yesterday, line 21, you say that the house burned down. And on page 4, last paragraph of the Serbian version, in the English version it's page 5, paragraph 1, and in the Albanian version it's page 6, paragraph 1 -- [In English] I mixed two incidents. [Interpretation] When you were talking about Kole Duzhmani, which is on page 3 -- paragraph 4 of the English version, page 4, paragraph 2 of the Albanian version, that is where you refer to Kole Duzhmani. In the next paragraph you say that a Russian soldier was instructed to kill him, and then you describe how he was killed and that the house that he had been killed in was set on fire. Your testimony is that 19 days later you found this body, and you recognised the bullet holes in the body; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In his body and on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that in the month of April the body had not decayed within 19 days but the bullet holes were still discernible?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may be true, because in the room where his body was found had a cement floor. All the furniture in the kitchen were burned down, but the smoke in the room preserved the body. So the body might have been left there for months and end and it would still be in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the body had not been charred due to the fire.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 4, the last paragraph of the B/C/S version, in the English version it's page 5, paragraph 1, and in the Albanian version it's page 6, paragraph 1, you say the following as you refer to the remains of 74 persons that had been killed in a particular place and burned. This is what you say: "The traces of the burnt bodies were very clear, and so I could estimate that about 74 persons had been burned there." How was it that you established that at that particular spot they had been burned and then removed, because you say there were traces of burning there. You refer to these 74 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there along with some foreign teams which came from England and to other countries. First they came up to my house because my house was closer to the road and my brother's house was burned. So together with them we went and examined the places where people had been killed. When we went to Meja cemetery near the meadow there, we saw the bodies, the places where they had been burned, we saw traces there, and we saw also the automatic rifles. Very few remains had been left. And the foreigners took the remains along with the cartridges in 74 different places. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a question here. By cartridges you mean the empty of the cartridge, the empty of the cartridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mean the shells. Yes, the cartridge of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, at least that's what the English interpretation says, automatic rifles were found there as well. How many automatic rifles were found there, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant the automatic rifle cartridges, not the actual automatic rifles. They were spread all over, the cartridges, and the foreigners took -- picked up some of them, three, four, as many as they found, and put them in their bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand. I'm sorry if it's my mistake. How was it that you came to the number of 74? Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's easy for me explain. The foreigners, and I was there with them, went to every place and found whatever remains, little as it were found, and they saw 74 adjoining places of people with some remains, and they were burnt with gas oil, with petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were not the one who established the number of the bodies involved, but you found out from some foreigners, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was there with them all the time. How couldn't I know? We could find together all the remains of the dead bodies. The interpreter was there. So we picked up all the remains belonging to 74 bodies. We might have said 200, 20, but that is not true. We found 74 places with human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who these foreigners were at that particular location?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know. They were 22 different teams coming and going. I can't remember them. They took pictures of the place. They filled it with camera. So I can't remember. Seven and a half years have passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were these forensic experts or journalists? Please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that they were foreigners bringing along interpreters to help them. But other than that, I don't know whether they were experts or not. I didn't the right to ask them who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this happened? Roughly?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first say of liberation and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just conclude. You personally did not establish how many corpses there were, or charred bodies, and you cannot say who it was who established that and who we can check this with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can deduce from the evidence that the witness has given what are the appropriate conclusions, Mr. Lukic. There's no need to go over this matter again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly now. We're on the English version paragraph 5, page 4. At Albanian version, page 4 -- page 5, paragraph 4. You're talking about your fear, when you were afraid that one of the killed persons was your son and when you went to check whether he was there. You established that there were no members of your family there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not recognise any one of the victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. All of them were young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know all the people from your own village; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously, then, these were not people from your village. Rather, they were people from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How can you know that they were not KLA fighters?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they been KLA soldiers, they would have not have come to that crossroads on the road to Albania. They would have taken to the mountains. They were all innocent men, 16, 17, 18 years old. If they were KLA members, they would have been in the mountains. They were along with their families, with tractors and cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you know that in the hills, in the mountains there were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were kilometres away, maybe 10 or more kilometres away and not there in the vicinity of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, did you know that in the village of Nec there was a Mujahedin unit as part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I haven't seen such a thing. No, no. There hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the KLA set up checkpoints along the roads in your municipalities trying to prevent the flow of regular traffic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't come across such thing in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you move about in the Djakovica municipality during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gjakova is a kilometre and a half away. I have gone there for some emergency, but there were military checkpoints. Every 500 metres there was a police -- a military checkpoint, and there was no civilian movement around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If civilians didn't use the roads, how did they move about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone stayed at home, because they knew if -- if they had to go through a checkpoint, you either managed to cross alive or you -- you disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did children attend school?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could they get there through that military checkpoint? The children are children. There was -- there was no school for the kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, Mr. Pnishi, that the children did not attend school in 1998 and in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where there were checkpoints, they didn't go to school, but if the school was within the area where there were no police and military checkpoints, the children went to school. Otherwise, they didn't. But where there were checkpoints, they didn't go across. If they were within that area, then they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Mrs. Merita Dedaj, one of the OTP witnesses, stated in her testimony that she did attend school and that she had to go across checkpoint or through a checkpoint, would you believe she wasn't telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where she lived, I think the school is right in the middle of the village, so she could go to school, but I'm talking about the area where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Or Ms. Merita Dedaj told us that she did attend school and that she had to go across a checkpoint. In your view was she telling the truth or not, since I can see now that you know which routes she moved along and where her school was. And according to her testimony, she attended school in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Korenica to Gjakova there were four checkpoints. If there was another road to the school without checkpoints, that's possible, but on the other side there were no checkpoints on the other side from there because there were not many people living in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pnishi. I won't dwell on this topic any longer. Thank you, Mr. Pnishi. This exhausts the questions I had for you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say something if I may. Just two words if you -- I wanted to say a word. If they have questions -- if they have questions, let them be quicker in asking them, because the sugar levels, I've got them up to 18, and I do not feel well. I've got a problem with diabetes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi had some treatment at lunchtime for his diabetes, and there was always the possibility that he would begin to be unable to deal with questions. So if you could continue as quickly as possible, within reason, then that would be helpful for the moment. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to be as efficient as possible, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps it would be good to have a break now since I don't believe the witness feels very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you feel unable to continue, Mr. Pnishi, or do you wish to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pnishi. My name is Aleksander Aleksic. I'm an attorney-at-law, and together with my team I appear on behalf of General Nebojsa Pavkovic. I have but a few short questions for you since I believe my learned friends dealt with most of the questions previously. Just a couple of things stemming out of your testimony today. On page 60, line 10 of the transcript, you stated that NATO did not bomb Cabrat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO did not bomb Cabrat. They would have gone bombing Cabrat if there was Serbian military targets to go after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, perhaps you can answer with a yes or no. It will go quicker. How far is Cabrat from Jakoc [phoen]. What is the distance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What if I told you that mount or hill Cabrat was bombed nine times between the 24th of March until the 10th of June? It was bombed on nine occasions and it received 84 hits by projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been there to visit. The people who went to that area, they died because of the mines. The area was mined. I didn't go to the area where you say there was bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, yesterday, I believe during your examination-in-chief, you made markings on a map and you explained what villages fell into the Carragojs Valley. Can you tell me what the distance is between Jahoc and Dobros?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobros.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dobros.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 10 kilometres, but there are other villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, in your testimony today, in response to my learned friend Mr. Lukic's answer on page 66, line 1, you stated that the KLA was in the hills, and then a few lines below that you said that they were up to 10 kilometres away in the hills. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In hills and mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Up to a distance of 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 10 more or less. I don't know the places exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, just one more thing regarding your statement. In the Albanian this is page 3, the penultimate paragraph. In the English that is page 3, paragraph 2, and in the B/C/S the same. There you state -- describing the people who entered your house, you said, the remaining two spoke Russian. They wore the same grey pants and jackets as the Serb paramilitaries. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On that same page in Albanian, and it continues on the next page, you mention those Russian soldiers again, and I presume all of those soldiers you saw whom you qualified as being Russian wore the same uniforms as the Serb paramilitary forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Meja and Meja Orize, these are two different villages, are they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two villages joined to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So they are adjacent.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we please show P35 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This necessary for any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will ask a question if it assists. Is there a village or hamlet called Orize or is the village and hamlet called Meja Orize?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Meja and Orize. They are two villages joined to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- if he's talking about the Orize in Gjakova, it's -- it's a neighbourhood in Gjakova in a different place, but these are two villages joined to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination, but the map I have from the Kosovo atlas shows it as being separate. I believe it could be seen from P35. There is Meja and Orize. They are not merged. According to the map, there is at least two and a half kilometres in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have the witness's evidence on that and if you wish to contradict that with other evidence that can be done in your own case or through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe you will like what I have to say. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KAMENOVA
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, can you tell us something about your education? We know that you served as a police officer for 15 years. Did you have any specialised, any professional training?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I finished the high school, gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KAMENOVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in cross-examination that you saw who carried away the bodies from the scene of the killing of the seven young men and boys on the bridge. Who was it who carried away the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken by Hamdija Alitaj and his two sons, Halit and Sabit. They came, they loaded the corpses on the bridge, and they got the other two corpses which had fallen off the bridge, got them on board a tractor, and then they also followed another lorry with corpses. They went in the direction of Gjakova as far as we could see them. We saw them, and then we don't know what happened to the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak with Hamdija Alitaj at all?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with him, Hamdija Alitaj. He came and met us. He came to borrow a mower from us, but we know that he was a collaborator and we offered him one or two, how many he wanted, and he said, "I have loaded up to 412, 412 corpses here and in Korenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does this arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness went on and much explanation but his evidence was limited from him in cross-examination as to his observations in respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's confine it to that and not 412 corpses. But you also need to control the witness, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in cross-examination that the tanks shelled the villages and set fire to the houses. Two questions: Which tanks or the tanks belonged to which formation, and when was it that they shelled the village -- the villages, and set fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the tanks of the Serbian army, and they shelled from Cabrat to Babaj. From Ramoc they shelled Nec, from Boboj [phoen] to Nec to Ramoc. They had occupied some vantage points, and they shelled from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was it? Or approximate about when was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1999, after NATO started bombing. Even before there had been cases, there were cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Pnishi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave. And if you wish to consult the doctor before you go, he will be available for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we -- unless it relates to this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, Your Honour. It relates to calling in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will go briefly into private session till I raise one matter with counsel relating to investigations that are ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Although maybe I'd prefer to stay in private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, as I indicated I wanted to raise a matter pertaining to the ongoing issue of the OSCE ICG forms that came up in connection first with Ms. Mitchell and then regarding some of the other witnesses. We received, I think, a supplemental filing from the Lukic team concerning this issue today. We intend to file something hopefully by the end of the day in connection with that. I would like to read something from an email I had from one of my colleagues who has been working on this issue and seemed to understand it much better than I do, and just to give the Court that information, we hope our written filing can clear it up, but based on my experience so far -- maybe it's just me, but it's the kind of thing I have difficulty understanding, even when it's pointed out to me with the two documents side by side by our analyst and by one of our lawyers. I can grasp it for a minute or two and feel that I have it but when I try to convey it to a third person it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it not be -- if you're concerned that we decide something before you get a chance to address the issue completely, then we can perhaps deal with that. Would it not be better if the filings were initially completed and then we had a brief hearing with everything on the table because I -- I've just got a feeling that if you start embarking on oral submissions without having completed the filing process we're going to get into a ping-pong exchange that may not advance matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I'm fine with that, Your Honour. I was concerned that my oral submission might raise more questions than it answers because that's what's happened to me before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you complete the oral -- the written filing exercise, then I will raise the question of whether any counsel wishes to make any oral submissions before we take the matter further, although I see there may even be resistance to that suggestion. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just inform you that I've just received an e-mail that we have also made filings in accordance with your ruling. I don't know if anybody else would like to subscribe to this, but I think that as far as submissions are concerned, this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it was that filing that Mr. Hannis referred to, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, the Lukic team also had filed something late last night which, I believe, is what Mr. Hannis was referring to..

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is the one I had seen from the Lukic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lukic has already been filed and I think that ours is being filed as we speak, so you'll get it within a few hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will give you an opportunity to indicate if you feel a further explanation is called for orally or an expansion on the submissions is called for orally before we make and final decision on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our next witness will be Hani Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if the witness is here. I have some indication that he may be on the way from the hotel. I know he was here earlier this morning. He went home at lunchtime, and I think perhaps the victim witness had him on standby anticipating it was going to take longer than it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Scotland we never allow witnesses to go home at lunchtime on a Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Someone is checking, I take it, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am informed he is on his way. The hotel is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Close by?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- ten minutes. I'm told any minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, we'll be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you wanted to continue to wait or take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No we will wait, because of the -- because of the need for breaks, it's better if we carry on a little bit for the moment, if we have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In connection with our filing, Your Honour, I wonder if -- if Defence counsel might agree and Your Honour might agree that we could have until Monday to file that filing I mentioned concerning the OSCE and ICG issue. Since I spoke, I've consulted with my case manager and some information from my other lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you can take it that from what we've said that you're not going to be pre-empted if it takes you until Monday to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you can correct me if I'm wrong about this, but I thought the arrangement for further witnesses or future witnesses was to let us know on a Thursday, and I'm not sure that we've got a list for next week yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm informed that we did file it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we're filing -- and, Your Honour, we're filing our list of September witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I was more concerned about the witnesses for the beginning of next week -- or for next week, rather, and whether there were any other than Peraj listed and whether you intended perhaps to change the order or whether he is likely to be the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we had anticipated that he would be the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then we have several others listed to follow him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's important to us from the point of view of preparation where you're relying on already available written material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, in connection with Mr. Peraj, I understand the outstanding documents have been translated and disclosed to Defence today. While we continue to wait, Your Honour, I can introduce another new face on our side of the room. Seated to Mr. Stamp's left is Christa Bosch, an intern working with us on this case right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't also juggle and sing, do you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I've tried "Juggling for the Complete Klutz" without any success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, since there's this uncertainty. We will adjourn now. We'll take the break now until a quarter to, and we'll run for an hour and three-quarters when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha. Mr. Hoxha, can you please read the solemn declaration which is being placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hoxha, we have already received a statement which you gave, and we have also received material, a transcript from the evidence you gave before when you were here in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, but as with all the witnesses in this case, there is a phase in the procedure, a stage when you come to the Tribunal to give evidence even though you've been before. This case relates to different accused persons. They are represented in this instance by a responsible counsel who themselves will ask the questions rather than the accused themselves. What we would ask you to do is listen carefully to each question that's posed and answer that question directly to the best of your ability. If we think that any person is asking you an inappropriate question, then we will intervene. But if we don't intervene, then we simply ask you to answer whatever question is asked. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first person to question you then will be on behalf of the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hoxha. I understand, sir, that you were born in Gjakova, and you've lived there all your life apart from your time in the military service and four years of university studies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your -- what was your previous employment?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: For -- I have worked for 40 years. In the first five years I was a teacher of primary school. For 35 other years I was a teacher of physical training at the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, I would like to show you a copy of your statement, which is Exhibit P2230. And I have a hard copy that I could hand to the witness. Mr. Hoxha, do you remember giving -- giving that statement to OTP investigators and verifying it before a court officer prior to this day?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I recall, sir, there were a couple of corrections that you noted should be made to -- to the schedule at the end with the list of people who -- who died on the 2nd of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's on page 14 of the e-court. Regarding the individual named Fetije Vejsa, where her age is listed as 80, 8-0, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. She was 58 to 60. Around this age, not more than 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the following page there is -- there is a young -- a young person named Silvana Vejsa. Is that the correct first name?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Not Silvana, Sihana.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with that, were there any other corrections?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: For the moment I don't seem to remember anything that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Other than that, sir, was -- were you satisfied that your statement is accurate and complete?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, but give me a moment to go back in time. My daughter Flaka, who was killed, was born in 1983. It's written here 15 years. She was 15 years. But she had turned 15. She was not yet 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: This is a detail that I wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is there a document making any correction here or are you just dealing with the corrections or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was just dealing with these corrections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As far as I know there has not been a previous addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, in late March, 1999, were you living in Gjakova with your wife and your 15-year-old daughter?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what part of town did you live in?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In the northern part of Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there a name for that area of town?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Abdurrahman Hajdar Pasha, number 2, is the name of the street where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, sir, in paragraphs 3 to 5 in the Albanian and on page 1 of the both the English and B/C/S at paragraph 3, you describe the night in about -- on about the 27th of March, 1999, when your neighbours Shefqet Pruthi and Avni Ferizi were killed. As to Shefqet, did you actually see him being pursued by his attackers?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that, but since there was only a wall separating him from me, his house from mine, I heard cries and shouts, and then afterwards his daughter told me, she had in fact called my daughter, my deceased daughter, telling her that they killed my father, and I saw only the dead body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And although you did not see that, I think you say in your statement that you heard shouts and insults in Serbian as well as a lot of gunshots. You're nodding your head, but we need a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I heard cries, insults, gunshots, but I didn't see that with my eyes. Later on, I learned what happened to Shefqet and to Avni Ferizi. In the case of Shefqet and Avni Ferizi, maybe his wife, his daughter might testify better than me. In the case of Avni Ferizi, probably his wife and his two sons might have testified better than me. I can tell you only what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. In connection with your eyes, I know you're wearing dark glasses in court today. I understand that's because of a medical necessity rather than any kind of fashion statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, it's not because of any fashion. These are prescription glasses, and I can't stand the light. I've been wearing these glasses since 1960. Dr. Cavka in Sarajevo prescribed those to me when I was a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now after this -- this happened, on paragraph -- in paragraph 8 of your statement, in English at page 3, paragraph 4 from the top, in the B/C/S page 3, paragraph 3, you explain that after your neighbours were killed on that night that everyone left that neighbourhood and that your 15-year-old daughter was very scared and upset, and you decided to go and stay with your oldest daughter. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: My elder daughter or the one living with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your elder daughter?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: My daughter's name was Tringa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you went to stay with her and her husband. Your son-in-law, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Lulezim Vejsa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So where -- where did they live? Where did you go to stay with them?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Their house is at a distance of 5, 600 metres from my house in a street called Milosh Gilic. I don't remember the name of their house now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at Milosh Gilic street -- Gilic? Sorry. You report in your statement that in all there were about 24 or 25 people spending the nights there at the end of March with the women and children in the basement under -- under the shop and the men standing guard in the courtyard or the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You go on to say that the first four nights were okay, but the night of the 1st of April and on into the early morning of April 2nd you describe what you say was the tragedy that happened to your family. Could you tell the Judges briefly what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: After the 1st and the 2nd of April, since we didn't have electricity and it was dark all over, panic reigned. And at that moment, we of course didn't look at the watch, but it was sometime after midnight. I was asleep, fully dressed. My son-in-law, Luli, together with his own son-in-law, Behar Haxhiavdija, who was here to testify in the case of Mr. Milosevic, came and woke me up telling me, "Wake up, wake up, because things are not good. It's not an ordinary situation." I woke up, of course, horrified, and my wife, my deceased wife, and both my deceased girls were a little bit further away. Their five children, Luli's sister with three kids, his uncle, Behar Haxhiavdija with his wife and three kids, all of them were staying in the basement. I woke up and went out in the corridor, and at that moment the -- someone tried to break in through the yard's door. Outside there was a car parked, and it was difficult for them to open the door, but finally they did open the gate and entered the yard. I can't remember the name -- the number, 10 or 15 probably, a group of armed people. At that time when I turned my back -- my head back, my son-in-law and his own son-in-law - that is the son-in-law of my son-in-law - I saw that they had disappeared. They were no longer there. Then I was hesitating as to what to do. Since my wife had told me, and also Luli's mother, and another woman, an old woman, a neighbour of ours had told us, "If something goes wrong you males should leave, because we are sure nothing wrong is going to happen to us females." At that moment, I decided to go back. I left the house and passed toward three walls and went to another house without knowing where -- whose house that was. I stayed there between two walls, in a crevice, so to say, until dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. And during that time you stayed there from after midnight --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From that time you stayed there from -- after midnight until dawn, what were you able to see or hear from the spot where you were?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I couldn't see anything because I was between walls, but I could hear voices, shots, cries, words, "Don't kill me, don't will me," which really made us feel very distressed. And the -- also the children. Even though they were in the basement and I couldn't communicate with them, and the next day I found them dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time you were -- you were between the two walls --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During this time you were between the two walls and you heard voices, I think you said, "Don't kill me," what language were those words spoken in?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want next to show you a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could bring up Exhibit P276.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, there should be a photograph appearing on your monitor shortly. I don't know if you can see that. Can you recognise what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What area is that?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In this corner here is the store of my son-in-law in whose basement those people I mentioned, my wife, my children, their children, were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. If I can have the usher help you. We've got a -- we've got a pen there which you can use to mark on the -- on this monitor in front of you. If you can draw a circle around the shop or the house of your son-in-law's that you're talking about. You can just touch the screen with the pen and draw a circle.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that the place where the women and children were staying in the basement?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the store I mentioned in whose basement all the people I mentioned earlier were taking shelter. In the back --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: -- Is the house where I was hiding, and my son-in-law and his own son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can -- I don't know, does it show on this photograph the area where you were hiding when you went -- went away from the house that night?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Approximately it is somewhere here. I left from this point and I followed this line. Somewhere here, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think it would be proper if it was further augmented with some numbers, 1, 2, 3, as in other exhibits, so one knows what it is meant for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, could you first of all put a 1 inside the circle that you've indicated was the shop.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could draw a small circle in which you indicated you were hiding until dawn, and write the number 2 in there.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hoxha. In case I misunderstood you, where you've marked a circle now was -- the area that I thought you had testified to was being the home, the home next to the shop. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Near number 2 is the house. Now it's ruined because it was burned, but it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you draw another circle in the spot where you were hiding until dawn and put the number 3 in that circle.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: 1 and 2 -- number 1 is 100 per cent accurate. Number 2 is almost 100 per cent accurate. Whereas the place I was hiding, I'm not 100 per cent certain of the location. Maybe 1 metre more, 1 metre less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But with that explanation, that's fine. Thank you. In -- in that same paragraph in your statement that we were referring to, you mentioned that then when dawn came you went back to your son-in-law's house and discovered -- well, what did you see or what did you find when you returned there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I may describe that. At dawn, when I emerged from between those two walls, I came onto the courtyard of a house which even today I do not know whose was it, whose it was. And then in -- in a nearby house I saw a person whom I know. He's from Gjakova. And he asked me, "What do you want here?" When he saw me there.
