And I explained that in the evening I was at Tringa's house, but at about midnight something forced us to leave because the forces entered the courtyard of my son-in-law, and I jump the two walls and I hid between the two walls. And I went together with him to the place where I was initially, and hoping that we'd find everybody else alive, my wife and the rest. I went directly to the basement where all the people were sheltered. I saw no one there. I saw that only smoke was coming out of there. I returned, and as I was returning, behind the shop there was a small house. The uncle of my son-in-law lived there, and unfortunately that man was not normal. And I saw his body charred. When I saw his body that was charred, I feared the worst for my family and the rest. Together with my neighbour, we went to our place and we saw that it was completely burned and ruined. The man who was with me, he said at one point that he saw a piece of flesh from a body, and at that moment we were convinced that a tragedy, unprecedented tragedy had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I stop you there, Mr. Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That moment Luli and Behar came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see your wife or daughters alive again? I understand that shortly after that you talked with a young boy who had been in the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was no answer to your question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I heard an answer, but I see it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your answer didn't come out. Did you ever see your wife and daughters again? I'm sorry to ask you again.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, I did not see them it alive. I wanted to discover what happened. And all this extraordinary tragedy, there is one thing which is still haunting me, because I haven't found out what happened, and -- and I did not want to see them in the condition they were after they were massacred, because I now only preserve the best memories from when they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about that. You didn't later that day talk to a young boy who had been in the basement but who had survived. Don't mention his name, please. We're -- he's -- he has protective measures, and we will refer to him as K13. Do you know who I mean, the young boy who survived?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I know who you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to talk with him afterwards about what had happened in the basement that night?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Briefly, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: When we found that there was an extraordinary tragedy that happened there, together with Behar I went on this other side to -- to the house of the grandfather of K13. There I met the young man, the boy, who at the time was 11. At the time, his father joined. He came in. This boy, in tragic moments, in critical moments, he was present where all the tragedy took place. When all these people were being executed, he says that, "The first, it was my daughter Flaka who was killed." K13, as a wise boy, for a moment he leaned against Manushen Duqi [phoen], who was another of the executed, and she was quite corpulent, and he lied as if dead, although he was wounded. I don't quite remember whether it was on his left or right arm. At the moment it was -- when everyone was executed, with the exception of K13, someone said, "Job done," and they left. At that point, they set the house alight. And when -- when the fire was taking over, they left. And when they left, K13 jumped out of one window and went to the house of his grandfather. And when I met him, he described all that had happened in detail, which to this day I do not want to believe what has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the name appears in the statement we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. It's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the statement will be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would -- we anticipate having this witness testify later. There's a possibility that he may not require these measures any more. If he does, what I would propose to do is -- is provide a substituted page with his name redacted or blacked out where it appears in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as of what date will this statement become public?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suppose that might be today, in which case I should provide a redacted page before the end of the day. May I consult with my -- may I consult?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the moment, Your Honour, perhaps I could request that we could tender this statement under seal and we'll provide a redacted copy later today or tomorrow -- on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Is it only -- there's more than one reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is more than one reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The whole package, since it's one exhibit, will be held under seal until you tender the redacted version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, then I want to --

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: A small correction, please. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the name on the screen, my name appears as Hannis. My name is Hani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my name is Hannis. I think that's where it happened, Mr. Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are references to the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your name on the transcript, that you're obviously able to read in English, is "The witness,".

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or oftentimes it appears as just as just A for answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, now I want to go to paragraphs 15 through 17 in the Albanian, and it starts at the bottom of page 4 in both the English and B/C/S. You tell us how you joined a large, long convoy of people leaving town that next day. Is that correct? Was that the following day or that same -- same day?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I joined the convoy of people on the 2nd of April at about 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was this convoy going?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Straight to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, you describe how at the town exit there were MUP soldiers -- or MUP policemen who were directing people to turn in their identity documents and put them in a large box there. Can you tell us how big a box this was?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: When we went out onto this road, we were walking towards the centre of the city to the old part of the city that was very beautiful, and there I saw that my city was burned, that Carsija was entirely burned. There we were walking over electric cables. We were walking over the waters which were coming out of the shops, and we could only see burned-out things. As we were leaving the city between Gjakova and the village of Brekoc there was a police checkpoint. There was a table and a big case where all the ID documents were thrown. Me personally, when they asked me for my ID, I -- I handed that to them and they took it aside and they put it in the box. Three or four kilometres after that, we were asked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. You were only asked one thing. We have all this in writing. All you were asked was how big was the box. Now, can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One by one metres. A cubic metre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you see how many documents were in the box? Was it 10? Was it a hundred? Any idea?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Sir, at -- at that moment I had lost my daughters and my wife, and I wasn't focused on such detail. And I wouldn't wish anyone to have to go through that. But up until the time that I was there, there were probably 3, 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Did the policemen who said that the documents should be turned in say why?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. They only asked us to hand in the documents and to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, I think you indicate further along when you got closer to the border with Albania you and others were again requested to turn in ID documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: They probably thought that they had not collected our IDs as we exited the town. And further away there was another checkpoint, and they asked everyone to go through the same procedure. But I told them that I had no ID on me because I had turned it in to a previous checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who was manning that second checkpoint? Was it soldiers? Was it police? Was it civilians?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In Kosovo you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, before you got to Albania.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: It was only policemen. In that particular checkpoint, it was only policemen. But in that meadow where we stayed for a while, there were soldiers who were everywhere around us, and there were thousands of people who were asked to stop there in that meadow, and there were soldiers around us who did not allow the civilians to move from the place, from the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hoxha, there's only one other question that I want to ask you in light of something that came up recently. You were a teacher for 40 years?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you teach in Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The last 35 years in Gjakova. The first five years, two years in Rahovec, near Gjakova, and three other years in a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard some evidence about the schools in Gjakova in 1999. Were the Albanian high school students able to attend school in Gjakova, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The high school students, and I was deputy director of one of the high schools, we could -- we couldn't teach the -- the students in the school premises, in the proper school premises, but we taught them in mosques and houses and elsewhere because we could not do that. And in my city, only 2 per cent were non-Albanians. It was between 1991 and 1995. We were not allowed to get into the proper premises of high schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what happened between 1995 and 1999 with regard to the schools in Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The situation was like this between 1991 and 1999. We were not even paid. In the last eight years, I got 40 Deutschmarks, which were coming from the contribution of the Albanian population who contributed by 10, 15 Deutschmarks. And in the last eight years, I -- I got about 40 Deutschmarks a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why were you not allowed to teach in the proper school premises?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: It's -- these gentlemen on -- in this room will know better that, the answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain any further? What was your understanding about why you weren't allowed to?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The reason why we were not allowed, I think these people know better than -- better than myself, but they probably wanted us to use our own programmes. There were differences between the programmes they had and ours, but the main thing is that they did not allow us to proceed, to teach normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no other questions. I would like to tender his statement and also the photograph that's been marked. If that can be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It will be IC7, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit IC7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's P2230, and that's tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would also like to tender the transcript from Milosevic which is P2231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We will proceed in this order for cross-examination General Lukic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, and General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hoxha. My name is Dragan Ivetic, and I am one of the attorneys representing Mr. Sreten Lukic, together with my colleagues, Mr. Branko Lukic and Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic. I intend to ask you a few questions this afternoon -- to clean up -- to clear up a few areas of your testimony. So please bear with me. I'll try to be as brief and concise as possible. Now first of all, sir, when talking about the tragic deaths of Mr. Pruthi and Ferizi, and I apologise if my pronunciation is inaccurate. You said that the spouses of these gentleman would know better than you what happened. Is it -- I want to verify that it's correct that you are not a personal eyewitness to the tragic deaths of these individuals that you testified about in your direct examination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I did not witness their execution, but Avni Ferizi is a best friend of mine. He graduated from the university in Belgrade. He -- and he's my best friend. He was my best friend. And I -- I have seen his body until it was buried. I cannot say here that I saw when -- I saw it when they were being executed. It was the wife of Avni and the wife of Shefqet who witnessed the execution, and they can testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, as far as the attackers or the perpetrators of these tragedies against -- the killing of these two individuals is it accurate to state, as you set forth in your statement, that you could not identify or distinguish the uniforms being worn by these individuals?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The night when Shefqet and Avni were executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I'm very clear. When Avni and Shefqet were executed, I didn't see the people who did that. The next day, before I took Shefqet and Avni to be buried, the wife of Shefqet and the wife of Avni, they went to the police, because when -- when I came close to the neighbour of Shefqet, and I asked them, "Why didn't you put the bodies inside?" They said probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would be easier if we do it in question and answer. That way we can at least get through the statement and complete your testimony. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the problems here, though, is that both the questions you've asked so far are questions which are clearly answered already, and one has to wonder what the purpose of asking for confirmation of something which is clear. And it's not surprising that the witness feels the need to expand upon it. He must think you're asking him something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was just trying to confirm some things that to me were not clear from the transcript, Your Honour, although they appeared clear in the statement. I just wanted to make sure that the statement was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the -- to the -- to the individuals that broke into your courtyard, would it be also accurate to state that you did not -- could not identify the uniforms that these individuals were wearing as well?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In my courtyard nobody entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic, sir. You started talking about how the spouses of Mr. Pruthi and Mr. Ferizi went to the police. Now, you did not accompany them on that occasion, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you, sir, do not know whether they reported to the SUP, that is the police station in Djakovica, or whether they reported to the local security organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. They went to the police, and they came back, and they told me that, "We went to the police to report the killings, and we are waiting for them to come." And they stayed in the courtyard of Avni Ferizi together with the brothers of Avni Ferizi. In the meantime, the police turned up, and they -- and they had a quick look at the body of Avni Ferizi and they left. This is what I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, and now do you know whether the regular police or the local security carried out this investigation into the death of the individual?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The regular police with flak jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at -- at the time in question, isn't accurate to state that there was also a local security force in the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: There was a very small group, but no one of the members was from Gjakova. As far as I know, no one from -- was from Gjakova. They were from the surroundings. Seven, eight, to ten people altogether. All my life I've been a happy, a friendly, a sociable person, and I -- I don't know anything about police matters. I know that my daughter, she learned Serbo-Croat through television.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at -- in your statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor, in the English version at page 4, paragraph 7, in the B/C/S, page 4, paragraph 7, in the Albanian, page 5 paragraph 7. In the middle of that paragraph, at least on the English version, you talk about the -- this local police force and say that, "However, this local police unit consisted only of local Serbs who spoke Albanian well." Now, I have a question to ask you about this local security force, the local police force as you call it, and I'm going to ask you if you know that in fact this local security was set up by the municipality of Djakovica rather than by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you have that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, I don't know who set that up. It was not only the Territorial Defence of Gjakova. They consisted not only of Serbs but also a very small number of Albanians. I must say this as well: According to all data, there was no -- not a single Serb who lived in Gjakova who was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, just for clarification, you started talking about the Territorial Defence. I'm focusing on this local -- what you have called the local police unit, which I referred to as local security, and in your statement this section that I've just cited, you indicated that this unit consisted only of local Serbs. Is that still your testimony, or is this part that you've just testified to relating to this local police?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The so-called local police force existed, and there was some Albanians who were part of it. I don't know exactly what number it was. I'm not interested in that. I am here to testify about what I have experienced in my family, the loss of my wife and two daughters. They -- I have also said that in another interview with the Albanian television that they have burned my house, which -- which I had built with my own efforts for 40 years. It meant that I gave. My wife was killed on the 10th of May 1999. My house was set on fire, and within that statement I will answer anything you ask me. Whatever I'm saying here, I would be the happiest man alive if it were not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and I appreciate that. I'm just trying to obtain information from you relative to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, which -- which is relevant to the proceedings in this matter. Now, Mr. Hoxha, do you in fact know or -- strike that. Would you be surprised to learn that the overwhelming number of these local security units in Djakovica, approximately 40 out of 53 members, were actually ethnic Albanians or other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I do not believe this comment. And even if -- even if there was a number of Albanians in this force, they were controlled and collaborating with the Serbs and were just implementing orders coming from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've mentioned that -- that there -- these Albanians would be collaborators with the Serbs. Would it be accurate to state then that there was an element of the ethnic Albanian population in -- within the entire municipality of Djakovica that was loyal or supportive of the Serbian state authorities?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I -- I don't know about these things. I know that many policemen, Albanians who were part of the regular police force, later on they -- they left the force because they were not willing to obey orders which would be against their own fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, within the various communities of the Djakovica municipality, isn't it a fact that there was some animosity towards -- strike that, some animosity between the part of the Albanian community that was loyal and supportive of the Serbian authorities and the remainder of the Albanian community in Djakovica? And I would reference you to the time period of early 1999, that is to say prior to April of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I'm going to object. I don't think we've established yet that there was some portion that was loyal, at least from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we have, Your Honour. I think he testified that -- I'll scroll back on my transcript here, but he talked about the so-called local police force and that there were some Albanians who were part of it, and I believe then afterwards he talked about how they -- these were collaborators with the -- with the state. So I believe that -- at least that establishes that. I'm sure the witness can clarify if there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll allow the question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to clarify. This is a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Hoxha. Just a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to have interrupted you, Mr. Hoxha. Please carry on with your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is nothing to clarify with respect to this question. I don't want to sound brutal and severe, but I regard it as a kind of provocation or a provocative question, because I'm not the person to answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise if you view it as provocative. It was not meant in that manner, sir. I'm just trying to elicit information relative to the region that you resided in that may be probative and relevant to these proceedings. Now, sir, you -- in your statement, I believe you stated that you had seen this local -- you call it local police. I'll call them local security. Isn't it a fact that this local security had different uniforms from the police based on your knowledge of having seen them prior to the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: As they had different uniforms from the ordinary police, but I don't think they had good intentions towards us because they have put us to torch. They have harassed my students. They have beaten them. They have not allowed them to go to the village. These are unpleasant things. So there is no way I can see them as police who protected the integrity of ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you're talking about the local security forces. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The so-called local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: They didn't let us go and buy bread -- prevented from going out to buy bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement, in the Albanian it's page 7, paragraph 2 from the top, in English page 5, the third paragraph from the top, and in B/C/S, page 5, the third paragraph from the top. In the middle of that paragraph sir, you state and I'll quote the English version "When the Serbs were killing people in my town, Gjakova, and burning houses, they were saying: 'This is because of NATO.'" Now, the question I want to ask you, sir, is with respect to this -- with respect to this particular recitation, this is not something that you were an eyewitness to, is it?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I haven't said this in my statement. Maybe it's the translator who hasn't put it right, but this was said by the wives of Avni Ferizi and Shefqet Pruthi after they returned from the police where they informed them of the murder of their husbands, because the police told them, "NATO killed your husbands." One of them said, "It was not NATO who killed my husband. It was you." This is what I have cited. But not at a single moment have I stated this as if I myself had said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you on the seventh page of your statement, the second paragraph from the top in the Albanian version? Is that the section that you are looking at that I was referring to? Are you telling us that those are not the words that you stated to the Prosecutor during this interview dated -- now, my copy says 1939. That's obviously a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Which paragraph was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Albanian version, it's page 7, and I believe it's the second paragraph from the top, and at least in the English version the text appears in the middle of that paragraph. I don't know where it appears in the Albanian exactly apart from identifying the paragraphs. Perhaps Mr. Hannis can assist maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could read the first line of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first line of the paragraph in Albanian is, and I apologise for my pronunciation: "Ulagava Nedja Shiptar Raskindia Kolonus ..." [phoen] And the section that I'm quoting comes in one, two, three -- towards the end of the fourth line of the Albanian version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 7 in my version I can't find it. But I know of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he has the -- he has the 92 bis package which has the attestation on the front. I think it's the paragraph right before he starts listing the names of all the victims. That will help him find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It is the paragraph just before you list the names of the victims of the tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the English version it's page 5, paragraph 3 from the top which is towards the second half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I step over and assist, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that yes mean that you do recall now having stated these words to the Prosecutor during the course of your interview?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. I meant that you go on with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you earlier stated that you did not -- you did not believe that you had made these statements in your interview. Seeing them recorded here at this section, do you now recall whether in fact you uttered these words to the Prosecutor during the course of your interview? That is to say, is this part of the statement accurately reflecting what you recall telling the Prosecutor on this topic?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: What is written in Albanian is what I have said, and I abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Now, I return to my original question. These words that you uttered, you were not an actual eyewitness to - let's break it down - Serbs killing people in your town, were you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And further, you were not an eyewitness to the other things that are listed in this sentence that we talked about. Is that accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: What do you exactly mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the burning houses and saying, "This is because of NATO." I'll just limit it to that.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: These are words which we have heard through television, through people speaking to each other. It was a very widespread idea that the forces that committed these crimes alleged that they did it because "you wanted NATO to come, and that's why you are suffering now."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think it's clear now. Now, sir, you testified that as you exited the city of Djakovica there were police officers at a checkpoint. Did you recognise any of the police officers, their identities?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you, very much, Mr. Hoxha, for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must disappoint you, but I have only a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hoxha, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, I am one of the people defending General Lazarevic, and I have just a couple of questions for you to clarify some things that arose during my learned friend, Mr. Ivetic's cross-examination. As far as I understood your statement and you were testimony today, you said that the police on the other, the send checkpoint before the border, asked to see your documents, your ID; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you told them that you had already given those papers at the first checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they try to verify that in any way? Did they try to search you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: When I was going to Albania, by pure chance in another pocket I found my driver's licence, and I even have it up to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, no one tried to verify that and you were not searched; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. No. They didn't have time because there were thousands of people waiting there. And if they were to each of us personally, it would have taken months. They didn't have the time. There was a column of about 10 or 15.000 people. It would have taken a week for them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, it suffice -- you said you simply turned over your documents even if it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: But I did turn them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But I hope you will agree with me that you could have told them that you had turned the documents over and they still wouldn't check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object. That calls for speculation on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing further from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hoxha, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my thanks to everyone for using every effort to complete these two witnesses today. That brings us the proceedings for the week to a close. We will resume on Monday. The sitting on Monday will be at 9.00 and will be a normal morning session finishing at 1.45 and divided by two short breaks of about 20 minutes, one at 10.30 and the other one about 12.20. The rest of next week the sittings will be in the afternoon, from 1.45 -- oh, sorry, from 2.15, and on a similar basis. Next week sometime we will issue a schedule setting out the sitting arrangements for a longer period insofar as we can and showing when there will be any interruptions in the proceedings as well so that we give as much notice as possible to enable you to make use of any gaps and also to plan your administrative arrangements around the sittings. So I hope everyone has as pleasant a weekend as possible in the circumstances, and I will see you all again on Monday at 9.00.
